summary:
Astronaut Health Guardian is an AI-assisted, offline-first health monitoring platform designed to help astronauts monitor their health during long-duration space missions.

The system brings health, wellbeing, radiation, and environmental indicators into a single dashboard. It tracks personal baselines and historical trends, helping astronauts identify unusual changes and understand potential warning signs through explainable alerts.

The platform is designed to work with limited connectivity, allowing important information to remain accessible offline and synchronize when a connection becomes available. It also provides a foundation for integrating NASA space-life-science data and approved mission sensors.

The project focuses on supporting astronauts in evaluating and acting on their health status, which directly addresses the NASA Space Apps Challenge objective for this challenge.

The current prototype is a web application built with React, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, Python, and FastAPI. It is designed as a monitoring and decision-support tool, not a medical diagnostic system.

The same approach could eventually be adapted for remote and isolated environments on Earth where reliable connectivity and healthcare access are limited.
details:
Astronaut Health Guardian

Astronaut Health Guardian is an AI-assisted, offline-first health monitoring software designed to help astronauts monitor important health and environmental indicators during long-duration space missions.

What does it do and how does it work?

Long-duration space missions can expose astronauts to challenges such as space radiation, isolation and confinement, altered gravity, cardiovascular changes, bone and physical health changes, behavioral health challenges, and changes in the spacecraft environment.

Our system provides a centralized health dashboard where astronauts can view health indicators, environmental conditions, personal baselines, historical trends, and potential warning signs.

The system organizes health and environmental measurements into an easy-to-understand dashboard. It compares current measurements with an astronaut's personal baseline and analyzes changes over time. When an unusual value or trend is detected, the system generates an explainable review flag so the astronaut can understand what changed and review the appropriate health procedure.

The project is also connected conceptually to NASA's Open Science Data Repository (OSDR) and its visualization resources. NASA OSDR contains spaceflight and space-relevant physiological, behavioral, biomedical, and environmental data. NASA's Environmental Data Application provides ISS-related environmental telemetry and radiation data such as temperature, CO₂, relative humidity, and radiation measurements.

The prototype can use NASA-derived reference data where appropriate, while simulated data is used for health indicators that are not directly available from public mission datasets. This allows the system to demonstrate the complete monitoring workflow without claiming that simulated values are actual astronaut medical measurements.

The application also follows an offline-first approach. Important information can remain available locally when connectivity is limited or interrupted, and stored information can be synchronized when a connection becomes available.

The system is designed as a monitoring and decision-support tool, not as a medical diagnostic system or replacement for professional medical procedures.

What benefits does it have?

The main benefits are:

  • Provides astronauts with a single location to review multiple health and environmental indicators.
  • Helps identify unusual changes and trends earlier.
  • Uses personal baselines instead of relying only on generic thresholds.
  • Provides understandable explanations for alerts and review flags.
  • Combines physical health, behavioral wellbeing, radiation, and environmental information.
  • Helps astronauts understand health changes in relation to their surrounding environment.
  • Supports low-connectivity and intermittent-connectivity environments.
  • Keeps important information available through offline storage.
  • Provides a foundation for future AI-assisted anomaly detection and personalized monitoring.
  • Can potentially be adapted for Earth-based remote and isolated environments.

NASA's OSDR also supports the reuse and analysis of space-life-science data across different studies, making it useful as a scientific data foundation for future versions of the platform.

The system is intended to support awareness and decision-making. It does not diagnose diseases or replace astronauts' official medical procedures and professional medical support.

What is the intended impact?

Our intended impact is to give astronauts a clearer, more proactive, and more understandable way to monitor changes in their health during long-duration missions.

Instead of viewing health measurements as isolated numbers, the system connects multiple indicators with personal historical trends and environmental context.

For example, an astronaut could view health trends alongside environmental conditions and radiation-related information, helping provide a broader picture of changes occurring during a mission.

The system can help astronauts:

  • Recognize unusual changes.
  • Understand personal trends.
  • Review appropriate procedures.
  • Communicate useful information to medical and mission-support teams.
  • Continue accessing important information during connectivity interruptions.

In the future, the same approach could be adapted for remote research stations, isolated workplaces, remote healthcare environments, and other locations where continuous connectivity is difficult.

What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software were used?

The prototype was developed as a lightweight web-based application using:

  • Frontend: React, TypeScript, HTML, CSS
  • UI: Tailwind CSS
  • Backend: Python and FastAPI
  • Database: PostgreSQL
  • Offline functionality: Progressive Web App (PWA), Service Worker, and IndexedDB
  • Data analysis / AI: Python and machine-learning libraries such as scikit-learn
  • NASA data/resources: NASA Open Science Data Repository (OSDR) and NASA OSDR visualization resources
  • Development: Visual Studio Code, Git, and GitHub
  • Deployment: Web-based cloud deployment

NASA's OSDR provides multiple data categories, including physiological, phenotypic, behavioral, biomedical, and environmental telemetry data. Its visualization suite includes tools for environmental and radiation data.

The current prototype uses a combination of NASA-referenced/available space data and simulated demonstration data, depending on the measurement being displayed. Simulated values are clearly treated as demonstration data rather than real astronaut medical measurements.

No specialized hardware is required for the current demonstration. The architecture is designed so that approved wearable devices, spacecraft sensors, or other authorized data sources could be integrated in future versions.

How is your project creative?

The project combines several ideas into one astronaut-focused health monitoring platform rather than concentrating on only one health measurement.

Our creative approach includes:

1. Personal Health Baselines

Instead of treating every astronaut the same, the system can establish an individual's normal range and identify changes relative to that baseline.

2. Multi-Dimensional Monitoring

The platform brings together health indicators, behavioral wellbeing, radiation information, physical activity, and environmental conditions in one interface.

3. Explainable Alerts

Instead of simply displaying a generic "Warning," the system is designed to explain what changed and why the astronaut should review the information.

4. Offline-First Design

The application is designed to remain useful when communication with Earth is limited or temporarily unavailable.

5. NASA Space-Life-Science Resources

The project uses NASA OSDR and its visualization ecosystem as an important scientific reference and data-resource layer. NASA's Environmental Data Application can visualize and compare ISS environmental telemetry and radiation data.

6. Future AI Integration

Machine learning can be used to identify unusual patterns, personalize monitoring, and prioritize review flags while keeping the results understandable.

7. Space-to-Earth Adaptability

The architecture is not limited to astronauts. The same concept could potentially support people working in remote, isolated, or low-connectivity environments on Earth.

What factors did we consider?

During development, we considered several important factors:

  • Limited and intermittent connectivity during space missions.
  • The need for fast access to important health information.
  • Differences between individual astronaut health baselines.
  • Long-duration effects of spaceflight on multiple body systems.
  • Space radiation exposure.
  • Spacecraft environmental conditions.
  • Temperature, humidity, CO₂, and other environmental factors.
  • Isolation, confinement, sleep, stress, and behavioral wellbeing.
  • Data privacy and protection of sensitive health information.
  • Security of stored and synchronized information.
  • Explainability of AI-assisted alerts.
  • Avoiding unnecessary or excessive warnings.
  • The possibility of false positives and false alarms.
  • The limitations of publicly available astronaut data.
  • The distinction between real NASA data and simulated demonstration data.
  • Future integration with approved medical, wearable, and spacecraft data sources.
  • Usability for astronauts who may need to understand information quickly.
  • The need for a lightweight system that can operate with limited resources.

Our goal is to create a lightweight, understandable, secure, explainable, and adaptable health-monitoring platform that can support astronauts throughout long-duration missions and potentially transfer useful ideas to remote environments on Earth.
